en: Not one remaining behind, all alone
The people of Jediger rode out,
And the black stallion, the fleet racer,
The foal of the miraculous gray,
The carved beauty taken as spoil,
The cudgel inherited from Toltoy,
When Surkön could no longer go.
The teeming black host of Jediger
Drew their bows like falling rain,
And shot their strange arrows like hailstones;
The foe surged roaring like a flood,
The raiders overran the land,
And when the enemy came roaring,
There was no luck anywhere in me;
Parted from Taibuurul,
Your princely uncle had no fortune.
When Surkön could go no farther,
I seized both his forelock
And his ears together.
To follow my father Manas’s path,
I dedicated him and slaughtered him.
In the blink of an eye,
Before one could turn this way or that,
Clouds arose from the hollows,
And over the summits of the mountains
Black clouds closed in,
The grass shook and quivered,
The princes fled in panic,
But is there any reason to flee?
Ah, ill-fated children, where are the people?
Will the day come when we reach them?
I sing and tell my song,
I tell my secret as truly as my faith.
My father’s confidant,
The lion Bakai, his comrade—
Can my grandsire still be safe and living?
Seize Kanchoro,
O wise man whose eyes have seen much,
Who has surpassed so many rivals.
A herald grown old among the people,
A saint from ancient times,
Whose valor is unlike another’s,
My heroic uncle Bakai,
My grandsire, elder of the people,
Has medicine in his pouch,
And all things beyond what others possess;
He has yet another remedy.
One medicine is called “Eбep,”
In dear Bakai’s hands
It used to soothe the aching place;
Another medicine is called “Sebep,”
It used to open eyes sealed shut.
Have him scour the face of the earth,
Mount him upon Jelmaian,
Clothe him in the Jekei-gray coat,
And have it fetched from Kakanchy.
Bring all his remedies;
From this infidel enchantress,
May he have the power to free us.
Before the five argali stars had set,
She had suckled him five times over.
His valor was extraordinary;
When his mother’s eyes failed,
They said he would vanish into the unseen.
Yesterday, when I was orphaned of my father,
She seated me upon the moon-gray steed,
And made Karakan flee before me,
Then spirited me away by enchantment
And brought my horse Buurul to me.
She placed my spear within reach;
Escaping from the sorceress,
Until I reached the far-flung people,
I could find no course of action.
She tethered the racehorse Buurul,
Kept me deluded and away from the people,
And placed a falcon in my hand.
She showed me Aigan,
And placed within my hands
The white sighthound Kumaıyq.
I turn my heart toward sorrow,
Unable to find what I should do,
I remain a captive.
Though without fetters or a net,
I remain bound.
I no longer count among humankind;
I remain under enchantment.
On every day of the week,
I go out for pleasure.
I have witnessed a monstrous thing:
For the sons of mortal men
I have yearned to rejoin them.
Led by Kökmonchok, eighty maidens—
So many wives from the unseen are mine.
If one says I died, I am not in the grave;
Though alive, I am not among the people.
Such filth has the world become;
My breast is aflame, my liver an ember,
And there is no soul with whom to share my secret.
“If Külchoro is alive,” I say,
And place my trust in the Creator,
While my heart blazes and my liver burns.
My two hands are bound,
My two eyes stare wide;
Such filth has the world become for me.
Princes wander distraught—
Is there any soul who should flee?
O children of this dark day, where are the people?
I shall bring turmoil upon your enemy;
I tell you this with certainty:
If my mother Kanykei is alive and well,
I shall stand as your support.
But if Kanykei is gone,
Climb the ridge and plunge from it;
In your renowned princely uncle
Place no further hope.
I shall be no homeland awaiting settlement;
If my mother has passed from this world,
Külchoro, I shall be no people to you.”
Thus spoke the mighty bloodthirsty lord,
When he gave this news.
Then the trusty giant Kara said:
“I shall speed over hill and hollow;
Hold him firmly and do not let go,
While I bring my mother Kanykei.
I shall scour the land stallion-like,
And not be gone longer than a mare’s milking.”
Saying this, the giant Kara
Spoke these words to Külchoro,
Telling a wondrous and astonishing thing.
Then the giant Kara
Seized the black-thonged whip,
Swung it round in his grip,
Pressed the surpassing steed
Hard between his knees,
And raced off, raising dust,
Galloping through Küröңsai,
Until he brought him to Talas.
They dressed them in costly garments;
Among horses none could catch Jeljetpes,
And before Jeljetpes
No racing beast could keep pace.
They mounted them on Jeljetpes,
Seated Kanykei and Bakai upon him,
And took them all away, leaving none behind.
Boundless in his swiftness,
The brisk and clamorous giant Kara—
He was both warrior and lion.
Wandering in flight across the plains,
The flesh of her soles worn translucent,
My dear mother Kanykei—
Can my aged mother still be alive?
If that mother of mine still lives,
And I become young enough to seek her breast,
If I suckle at her breast and sleep,
If I breathe my poor mother’s scent
And smell it day and night,
My eyes and ears will open.
The pain within me will subside,
And the enchantments around my soul will scatter and flee.
I shall pitch my camp beside you,
My awe-inspiring hero Külchoro;
Then I shall hear your words,
Then I shall see your face.
If she is safe and alive,
Send a letter to my mother;
If you send it, send it swiftly.
My venerable white-haired mother,
My destiny and homeland before me—
If my destined homeland still exists,
Let me open my eyes and see her,
Let me suckle at her breast.
Win honor by rescuing me from the wilderness;
My dear Külchoro, ride now.
With six swift horses,
And a letter small as your palm,
Search across the face of the earth.
Set scouts and search the land,
Search the people seven days without rest,
And find my mother.
If my mother comes within my sight,
If she gives me her true breast,
If I suck and milk flows abundantly,
I shall appear before her eyes,
And pitch my camp beside you.
I shall be a binding for your waist;
Choro, heed my words.
I shall be the standard that bears the banner,
Sobbing in grief,
Wailing and weeping bitterly,
What she had called early became late,
And in longing to see her dear son,
Her two eyes became four.
Her mind reeled and tears streamed,
Her heart surged and her senses fled;
To see the blue-maned lion,
To behold him and then die,
To turn her face toward God,
And surrender her entrusted soul,
Her spirit failed and her senses fled,
Bloody tears flowed from her eyes.
Snow veiled her bloodshot eyes,
Illness struck her blood-filled lungs;
Flying like an arrow and shrieking,
Kanykei had set out.
Now that Kanykei had grown old,
Upon the Kökcholok beneath her,
Striking the whip again and again,
That Bakai raced along,
Wrenching and tugging
At his mustache and beard in anguish,
Yearning to reach the blue-maned lion;
If he reached him, poor old Bakai
Was ready to sacrifice himself,
To part with his entrusted soul.
Your lion, Bakai,
Was ready to die before death’s appointed hour;
Your valiant grandsire Bakai—
Most of the old man’s life was gone;
See how hard he rode.
Before one could turn this way or that,
In the blink of an eye,
At the tent with the golden pillar,
They came and found
The bloodthirsty hero who had vanished.
The lost one was found,
The road opened and honor was restored;
Kanykei wept with piercing cries—
That man too was the finest of all.
They mounted him upon a chosen charger;
They had settled him there.
Driving the splendid black stallion,
They were leading him onward.
“My venerable white-haired mother,
My dearest mother,
The only one you cherished has been found,
And now your honor is restored.
What was broken in you is made whole,
What you lacked has been found.
Your hard bones have softened;
Your wasted body has grown stout,
Your hungry belly is filled,
And the hostile enemy is slaughtered.
Remain with us, Mother,” he said,
“My mother who cherished me.”
When she heard this news,
Your poor, passionate mother’s
Heart broke and flew apart,
And tears poured from her eyes.
She wailed and wept aloud,
Sobbing, unable to endure;
All the goodness became clear,
She burned fiercely in grief,
Her heart heaved and her eyes twitched,
Your dying mother rejoiced.
Her snow-white hair had thinned;
When her lost son was found,
